extracted.intended_audience: researchers, research-integrity professionals, science communicators, and concerned academics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and first-hand reflections on detecting, flagging, and responding to suspected scientific misconduct (image manipulation, paper mills, fabricated data) and on how stakeholders and platforms should act. Includes practical advice for volunteers, communicators, and institutions involved in research integrity work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder responsibility (everyone must play a role)
rubrics_metrics.description: It takes all the stakeholders — publishers, authors, funders, research institutes, vendors — to play a role in combating misconduct; no single actor can solve it alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elisabeth Bik emphasizes that publishers, institutions, authors and funders should all be involved; examples of failures occur when each party waits on another (journal waits for institution, institution gives vague replies). "It takes a village"—coordinated action is required to make the self-correction of science work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely and transparent investigation and response
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals and institutions must respond promptly and transparently to concerns about papers rather than sending vague statements or not replying at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple anecdotes where emails to journals or the Office of Research Integrity received no acknowledgement; anti-pattern is long delays or lack of outcomes. Guidance: reply, investigate, and communicate outcomes rather than leaving concerns unresolved for years.

rubrics_metrics.name: There must be consequences for misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: If people commit misconduct and suffer no consequences, honest researchers will leave science and misconduct will persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bik argues that having consequences is essential to deter wrongdoing; absence of sanctions allows 'bad apples' to remain and harms the field. Institutions and journals should ensure appropriate corrective actions (retractions, institutional investigations, sanctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use PubPeer (and public flagging) to warn readers when investigations stall
rubrics_metrics.description: When formal channels fail to act, posting concerns (e.g., suspected image problems) on PubPeer can warn readers to 'proceed with caution'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bik posts suspected image manipulation on PubPeer to alert readers that a paper may be problematic. This is presented as a pragmatic approach when journals/institutions do not follow up; it is a public caution rather than a definitive accusation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raise concerns as questions rather than accusations
rubrics_metrics.description: When contacting authors or journals, frame issues as requests for clarification (e.g., ask about IRB approval or control group composition) instead of outright accusing misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bik describes preferring to "raise concerns" and ask concrete questions so authors can respond; this approach helps avoid immediate defensive attacks and reduces legal risk. Example questions: 'Did you have IRB approval?', 'Can you elaborate on the composition of your control group?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the paper, not the person
rubrics_metrics.description: Make critiques about the evidence and figures in the paper rather than attacking authors personally to keep the debate evidence-based and avoid undermining credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bik intentionally points to problems in papers and tries not to single out individuals; she warns against messaging that could be interpreted as 'all science is fraudulent.' Keeping the focus on data and methodology reduces the risk of claims being misread as attacks on science as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers must proactively detect and deter paper mills
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should implement detection measures and collaborate (e.g., coalitions) to identify and stop paper mills that produce fake papers and sell authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bik describes paper mills as organized fraud producing many similar fake papers; publishers have become more aware and are taking steps, but it's a 'rat race' as mills get more sophisticated. Coalition efforts (e.g., STM) are noted; continued vigilance and improved detection methods are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use social media strategically — it's powerful but double-edged
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media can shine light on misconduct and amplify evidence, but it also spreads misinformation and can erode public trust in science if mishandled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bik calls social media useful for exposing problems ('Sunshine is the best disinfectant') but warns that the same platforms enable conspiracists and misinformation. Advice: use social media to highlight problems in papers, avoid sensationalist messaging, and be mindful of the broader impact on public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect personal safety and mental health when exposing issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who flag misconduct may face coordinated online attacks, doxxing, death threats, and legal intimidation; take steps to protect yourself and mental health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bik describes locking Twitter (making account private) temporarily, receiving legal threats, doxxing, and coordinated trolling. Recommended mitigations: limit exposure, use privacy settings, rely on community support, remain polite in responses, and consider your employment/security situation when deciding how public to be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on reputable information sources but remain skeptical
rubrics_metrics.description: Use trusted sources (PubMed, CDC, respected university pages, major newspapers that do fact-checking) for information, but recognize even reputable journals can publish flawed or fabricated work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bik lists PubMed, CDC, university medical pages, and the New York Times as trusted sources. Caveat: high-profile examples (Surgisphere in The Lancet) show even top journals can publish bogus data, so verification and critical reading remain necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn common failure modes from resources (Retraction Watch, PubPeer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Study Retraction Watch and PubPeer to learn typical forms of misconduct, image manipulation, peer-review rings, and other red flags to train yourself in detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bik recommends browsing PubPeer to see the types of problems posted and Retraction Watch to read follow-ups when investigations lead to retraction. She mentions the #imageforensics hashtag and a PubPeer plugin as practical tools to learn and track flagged papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer small-donor or independent funding models for unpredictable integrity work
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding via donations/Patreon can be preferable to structured grants because the work is tip-driven and unpredictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bik explains she uses Patreon donations for basic income and prefers not to rely on grants that impose artificial goals or plans; small recurring donations allow flexible, reactive work on unexpected tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid framing integrity work in ways that discredit science broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: When communicating about misconduct, take care not to give the impression that 'all science is fraudulent'—emphasize that most science is trustworthy while addressing bad actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bik repeatedly warns she does not want her work interpreted as an indictment of all science; she starts talks noting most science is good and underscores nuance to avoid fueling anti-science narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution/journal deferral is an anti-pattern (do not wait on others indefinitely)
rubrics_metrics.description: When journals and institutions each wait for the other to act, allegations can languish; proactive decisions and independent action are necessary to prevent stalemate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bik recounts cases where journals wait for institutions, institutions give vague promises, and authors move on—resulting in no outcome. Institutions and journals should avoid circular deferral and take clear, timely steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask for concrete evidence and verification in queries
rubrics_metrics.description: When querying suspected problems, request specific documentation (IRB approvals, raw data, methodology clarifications) to allow verification rather than relying on assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical examples include asking about ethical approvals, control group composition, or specific figure data. Concrete requests help determine whether issues are honest errors or misconduct and can prompt corrective action if warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platforms have responsibility to moderate misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Social platforms should enforce moderation policies (remove or flag misinformation and harassing content) because lack of moderation empowers misinformation and harms scientific discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bik contrasts platforms—Facebook and YouTube still moderate some misinformation, while recent Twitter leadership changes have reduced moderation, allowing reinstatement of harmful accounts. Effective moderation protects science communicators and public understanding.
